Mira packed on a Tuesday morning, in the front room, with the suitcase open on the horsehair sofa and the streaked window laying its slow gray bands across her back.

"Three nights," she said. "Manchester. The conference with the terrible coffee."

"Three nights," Dave said.

"Don't let the ghosts get lonely." She folded a blouse with the flat efficiency she brought to everything except him. "Or do. Let them have a party. Just don't let them use the good glasses."

"There aren't good glasses."

"There's a whole category of glasses you'd cry about if a ghost broke one. Work it out." She zipped the case and stood, and kissed him, and at the door she turned back and said, fondly, "Talk to your chair. It'll be good for you."

Then the door, and the taxi idling, and the house settling into its own silence the way water settles after a hand is taken out of it.

He had a week of things to do. He did none of them that first night. He made a sandwich, ate it standing up, and then walked the hall because the hall was where the boards spoke and the cold lived and where, in some sense he did not enjoy admitting to himself, the house kept its front door to whatever else was there.

At the end of it, by the back door, he stopped. The bulb buzzed above him. The streak in the glass lay under his palm like something frozen mid-motion.

"Right," he said, to the hall, in his ordinary voice. "Mira's away. So it's just us, and I'm not going to pretend I'm checking a fuse."

Nothing. The cold, at least, was there—flat and even, lying along the boards.

"I don't know what you are. I've got opinions. I don't know." He rubbed his thumb along the doorframe. "What I do know is, the other night. The phone. Her walking around filming you like you're a cheap trick." He was quiet a moment, and the quiet went on long enough that he could hear the water moving in the pipes upstairs. "That was rude. It was rude and I let it happen because it was easier than arguing. So. That's mine. I'm sorry."

On the second day the house began, unmistakably, to be polite.

He came down in the morning and the cold at the foot of the stairs was gone; standing where it had been was a warmth with no radiator behind it, a warmth like a door left open onto a room somebody had just left. The kitchen was as he had left it and the drawer was in its runners and the cutlery was in the drawer.

In the front room the chair he sat in to read—the one he had, left to himself, angled toward the window and the light—had been moved. But not moved the way it had moved before. It stood exactly where he liked it, on the boards, at the angle he would have put it himself after fussing, as though someone had watched him for a month and learned the measure of his eye.

The other chair—the one Mira had turned back to the corner—was square to the table, back to its place. Dusted. Nothing in the room was out of order. Everything in it was arranged.

"Thank you," he said, feeling foolish, and then not foolish, because the smell came up around him as he said it: camphor, and rain on stone, close and brief and clean, and then gone.

He ate breakfast in the front room with the light coming through the waves in the glass and did not turn on the radio.

---

On the third night he could not stay in his chair.

The hall was dim. The bulb above it had been turned down—no, he had turned it down himself, at dusk, out of a sense of consideration he did not have a name for. One weak light on faded green paper, and at the far end the streak of gray from the back door, and the boards, and the cold coming along the floor, and then, arriving before it, the scent. Camphor. Rain on stone. Strong enough that the hallway seemed to have widened.

He put his book down.

At the end of the hall, where the light was bad, a woman stood.

She had not come through the wall or out of the door. She was simply there, the way a thing at the edge of vision is there until you look, except that he looked, steadily, and she did not go. She was tall, and her dress was dark and long and had been good once—a housekeeper's dress, he thought, and did not know why he thought it. Her hair was up in the way of women in old photographs, and her hands were folded at her waist, and where the weak bulb reached her, her edges blurred, not like a photograph out of focus but like a figure drawn in ink that had been rained on. Around her face the light went soft, and the softness moved.

He could not see her eyes clearly, and he knew that she was looking at him.

His phone lay on the arm of the chair. His hand had gone to it without his deciding, and he had it up, thumb on the side, before he understood what he was doing.

"No," she said.

Her voice was low, and it had the particular dryness of a room that has been kept shut, and it cost her something to use it.

"Please don't," she said. "I have had enough of being looked at through glass."

Slowly—his ears going hot, absurd and ashamed—Dave put the phone down on the table, face down.

"All right," he said. His voice came out gravel. "All right. No glass."

She inclined her head. A small formal motion, terribly polite, the courtesy of a woman who had once been introduced to a great many people and had learned exactly what a head did at a threshold.

"You said good morning," she said, "to my stone."

"Yes."

"Every day. In rain, once, with your hat off." Her hands moved against each other at her waist. "Nobody has said my name in a long time. They read it, perhaps. Reading is not saying."

Behind her, at the window, the streaked glass held its smear of gray light. Dave found he was breathing carefully, in through the nose, and that the camphor was inside him now, warm at the root of everything and cold at the surface, both.

"I don't know what to call you," he said.

"Hattie."

"Hattie." He said it out loud, in the dim hall, and something eased in the air—the whole length of the hall seeming to let out a breath. "I'm Dave. This is your house. I'm sorry about the tape."

"Don't look away," she said. "That is what they all do. They look, and then they cannot manage it, and they turn to the wall and tell themselves it was the light." She came forward one step. The floorboard second from the door took her weight, and spoke, and this time it did not frighten him. "I have been so long without being looked at by anyone who would stay."

She came up the hall. The cold came with her, not the flat water-cold along the boards but a cold with a shape to it, arriving. He stayed sitting because his legs did not trust themselves, and because standing might have looked like leaving, and because—he would think about this later, and not know what to think—he did not want her to see him flinch.

She stopped at the arm of his chair.

"Your hand," she said.

He gave it. He held it out into the dim air of the hall, palm up, like a man asking a woman to dance in a room where the music has stopped, and the smell of camphor closed around him so strongly that his eyes stung.

Her hand came down. It was cold, and there was weight in it, and the cold went up his wrist and into his arm and sat behind his ribs, and it was the most alive he had felt in years.

Dave did not flinch.

**Mechanic the fifth — Engagement Rationing.**

This was supposed to be a throwaway aside. It has declined to be thrown.

Engagement Rationing is the rule that every reach for the number costs a small, unrecoverable piece of the day. Not a large piece. A *small* piece. A piece you would not notice if it happened once. You reach for the number — a refresh, a glance, a thumb moving before the thought arrives — and the day gets shorter by a unit the rulebook calls a “sliver.” Slivers do not accumulate visibly. They accumulate *actually*. At the end of a day of reaching, you have a day that is the correct length on the clock and a length short in the chest, and you cannot point to where it went, because the point is that you cannot point to where it went.

[Footnote 27: Slivers are non-refundable and non-transferable. You cannot give your slivers to someone who needs them. You cannot save them up. This is the cruelest thing in the document, and I say that as a person who has read the document four times and understood it zero times. It is cruel because it is fair. It is fair because it is priced. It is priced because the developers know that a person will pay a sliver for a glance, every time, and will call the payment “staying informed,” and will not notice the day getting shorter until the day is short.

I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. There is no balance. There is only the reaching.

And then I heard it.

Not a notification. Not a refresh. A *purr* — low, warm, structured, the way a sound is structured when it has been designed by someone who wants you to keep listening. It came from the edge of the post. The edge of the post is not a place a sound should come from. The edge of the post is a margin. I am aware that a person who hears a purr at the edge of his own post and continues typing is not a compliance clerk, he is *content*, and content is a §7.3 category, and I have been stamped today. I am aware. I am saying so. That is compliance. Not agreement. —The OP, who would like it noted that he is fine, and who would like the record to show that he hesitated, and who would like it very much if the record did not show how briefly.]

The queue for the chapel hall ran twice around the block by six in the morning, and Mira Vance stood in it with her hands pushed flat in her coat pockets, counting because counting was what she did instead of waiting. Thirty-one ahead of her to the corner. Then the corner turned and there were a hundred more.

Teo had taken Nell to the school hall, because Nell was seven and had insisted on her own mask, her own queue, her own turn, and because Teo had a caretaker's key and could get them in the side door before the crowd. Mira had kissed them both on the step and told Nell not to lose the strap. Nell had said she was not a baby. That was two hours ago, and the sky over the filter works had gone from grey to a paler, harder grey.

The Trust women came out at seven in grey tabards, with the crates on a handcart. There was a table and a stack of instruction cards and a woman with a stapler. The cards said: *Breathe normally. Twenty minutes. If you feel faint, sit down and raise your hand.* The woman with the stapler read the same four sentences aloud every ninety seconds, in a voice that had been taught to her at a course.

The hall smelled of floor wax and wet wool and forty years of hymnbooks, and under all of it, that faint sweetness everybody in Lowfield had agreed was the dust suppressant and had agreed you couldn't really smell. Mira got her mask at seven forty. It was lighter than it looked — cardboard and a soft rubber lip and a filter core the size of a tea tin — and it went on like putting her face into a small dry room.

She counted to twenty because she did not trust the card.

At eleven she noticed the woman behind her was breathing. Not the sound of breathing in general. That specific woman, her mouth, the small wet catch in it at the end of each exhale. Mira turned halfway and then made herself stop, because staring was rude, and the rudeness had come on her so fast and so plain that it startled her.

The room arrived all at once after that. The handcart wheels grinding on the flagstones. The stapler. A baby two rows back, not crying yet but deciding. Somebody's boot scuffing the same rhythm over and over. It had all been coming to her through wool her whole life, and now it wasn't, and the difference was so large that she put one hand on the table to steady herself and the Trust woman said, without looking up, "That's expected. Increased clarity. Report adverse effects at the desk."

Her chest hurt. Not the heart, the ribs. A pressure behind them, like a debt she'd have to sit down and work out with a pencil. Somewhere in the middle of it she thought the word *unpaid* and did not know why, and the not knowing was worse than the pressure.

She wept at the door, briefly, and it was ordinary weeping, the kind that comes and goes. What frightened her was that she wanted to put the mask in her pocket and walk back into the soft. She wanted it the way she wanted her bed after a double shift. She stood in the porch with her hand pressed to her mouth until it passed, and then she went to find the woman with the stapler and asked, very reasonably, whether there was a form for giving the thing back.

"There's no giving it back," the woman said. "It's a gift."

Jonah Idris had the vestry desk and a register and a target. Six hundred and twelve masks for this hall, seven thousand for Lowfield, and a memo in his folder that said the district would clear eighty-one percent of registered households within the three days, which was a number the Trust had decided in advance, the way it decided everything.

By four they had signed out four hundred and eleven. He kept the tally in pencil in the corner of the register, and every half hour the number went into a box on a form, and every hour the form went into a satchel and the satchel went out to a car.

The queue was mostly patient. That surprised him. He'd expected something worse, and instead there were old women with folding chairs and a boy who had brought his grandmother's wristband because she couldn't walk, and one man who argued about the twenty-minute rule and was wrong and gave up. People took what they were given. They always had, at the desk.

He went back to the storeroom at four-fifteen for another case of cores and found the reserve stacked against the far wall: Class C cores, sealed, stencilled, forty to a carton. He counted the cartons because he had been counting cartons since he was nineteen and it was the one thing he was good at. Sixty-one cartons. Two thousand four hundred and forty cores.

The memo had said eight hundred held in reserve for Lowfield.

He stood there a moment in the smell of rubber and cold stone, and he did not take out his pencil, and he did not ask anybody, because there was no box on any form for asking that question. Then he carried a case out and shut the door.

The weeping man came at ten past five. He had a household allocation form, two pages, and he had filled it in up to the third name, and his hand would not do the fourth. Jonah watched him for a while from the desk — the man's shoulders, the pen travelling to the line and then coming back — and then he went round and crouched by the chair.

"Which one?" Jonah said.

"Her name's the same as mine," the man said. "It's the same name as mine and I can't — " He laughed once, horribly. "Six years I've written it on forms."

Jonah took the pencil out of his hand and wrote *Elin*, guessing the spelling and guessing wrong, and let him correct it. The man signed. Then he sat with the completed form in his lap and cried without any attempt at all to stop, which by then everyone in the vestry had seen twice that day, and which Jonah had been told at the training was a normal transient response and should not be interrupted.

Jonah got him a cup of water. He thought, for no useful reason, about his mother, about the bus she took on Tuesdays to the Annex and the way she always came back with a folder of brochures and said, *They take wonderful care of us,* and he filed that thought away as he filed everything, neatly, in a place where it would keep.

Mira walked home the long way, down the river side where the laundry lines hung over the alley, and then she turned into her own street and stopped, because the house was there with its edges on.

She had lived in that house for eleven years. She had never once looked at it. The drainpipe at the corner had pulled loose from its bracket and hung a hand's width out from the brick, exactly as it had hung since the spring of last year, and Teo had said he would fix it, and she had said fine. The shutters were the wrong green. The gate hung on a hinge that made the gate open at an angle, and the step was worn into a shallow dish where the three of them came and went, and none of it had been decided. It had all just happened to them, quietly, in a soft room.

She could hear the neighbors. Not the general noise of a street, which she had heard all her life, but the actual thing: a man in the third block shouting at his brother, two women arguing across a fence about a debt, a child crying the way children cry when nobody is coming. All of it at the same volume. All of it meant.

The woman from number nine came out of her gate and stood in front of Mira with her mask held out by the strap, dangling, like something she'd found and didn't want.

"Take it," she said.

"It's yours."

"I want the old air back." Her face was wet and her jaw was working. "I've been standing in my kitchen since noon and there's nothing in there I want. Take it back to them."

Mira put her hands behind her back. "There's no giving it back."

"Then what's the point of them," the woman said, and went inside and shut the door too hard, and the sound of it went off in Mira's ears like a dropped tin.

She stood a moment longer in the road. Teo and Nell would be home by now, and Nell would be wild with the mask and bossy about the strap, and Teo would have something in the oven, and the three of them were going to sit down at a table tonight and be with each other without any of it being softened first. She was afraid of that. She had never been afraid of her own family before and she found she did not know where to put it.

Then, from the block behind her house — from the row that backed onto theirs, the one with the shared yard — the first scream came. High, and cut off, and then again, and then a man's voice saying *no, no, no* in the flat way of somebody who has just understood something.

Mira was running before she had decided to.

He began with the windows, because the windows were where a draft would come from. The front room's two tall sashes: he ran a strip along the meeting rail, pressed it flat, and felt the old glass cool under his palm. The streaks in it lay under the tape's shadow like something frozen mid-motion. Then the back door's streaked pane, and the small window over the sink, and the one at the top of the stairs that Mira said did not latch. He did the sills, the cracks, the gap under the back door where a draft could slide in flat as a hand. By noon the house had grown a second skin of tape and smelled of adhesive, and it seemed to him a reasonable smell, an evidence smell, the smell of a man taking the measure of his own foolishness.

Then the furniture. This was the part he was ashamed of and did anyway. A strip across the front leg of the reading chair and down onto the boards. A strip from the sideboard's corner to the plaster. A strip along the kitchen drawer front to the frame, and one on the drawer's handle. He used a pencil to draw a fine line at each join, so that a hair's movement would show. He was careful and quiet about it, the way he was careful about squaring a picture, and when he was done he stood in the hall with the roll in his hand and looked at what he had made of his home.

"Right," he said. "Now we'll see."

He set the lamp on the floor at the middle of the hall, plugged it in, and turned it on. Then he sat down against the wall with a blanket over his knees and his back to the faded green paper, and he waited.

The night was long and nothing happened in it.

He had not expected nothing. He had expected, honestly, a small spiteful event—a handle turned, a chair nudged, the bulb dying, some petty proof. What he got was a hall that had gone entirely ordinary. The bulb buzzed. The lamp threw a yellow circle on the boards. At two he got up and went round with a torch and checked every mark: the chair, the sideboard, the drawer, the windows. Every pencil line sat where he had drawn it, unbroken, exact. At four he checked again. He sat in the cold dawn light and felt the certainty of the last weeks begin to come apart in his hands like wet paper, and what was underneath was worse than ghosts. A man of thirty-eight, in a house that made noises, talking to a hallway. **§10.0 — THE INTERNET ENDGAME ZONE, WHERE THE FOG IS RANKED**

I am inside now.

There is no entrance sign. There is no exit sign. There is blue light, the exact blue of a screen at three in the morning, the blue that makes every face look like it is being audited. The fog is not weather. The fog is *ranking*. It rolls in low and sorts everyone by a number I am not allowed to see but am constantly told I should care about.

Everything here is scored. Arrival time. Reaction time. How fast you said you did not care about the score. There is a leaderboard for people who publicly announced they were leaving the leaderboard. It is the largest one. It is alphabetised. It is not alphabetical.

[Footnote 37: The fog does not lift when you stop refreshing. The fog lifts when you *stop needing the refresh to lift it*. This distinction has been filed under §10.0(c), “Conditions Players Describe as Unfair Because They Require Something Hard.”]

And through the glass — the wrong side of the glass, the side that used to be my side — I can see The Human Race.

Warm light. Ordinary chairs. The ticket machine, dispensing 12, then 4, then 88, then 12 again. The sign above it: NOW SERVING: EVERYONE EVENTUALLY. The chairs are empty. The lamp is on. Someone is reading in there and has not looked up, and I still do not know whether they cannot see me or have decided not to.

The lobby is not reachable from here. I want to say that plainly, because the fog makes it look close. It is not close. It is visible. Visible is not the same as close. Visible is a taunt with good lighting.

**§10.1 — SURVIVAL APPENDIX: SUB-RULES FOR PLAYERS STILL IN THE ZONE**

Each of these is a rule. Each of these is also a confession. I have stopped pretending those are different documents.

**Sub-Rule 12 — Do not refresh in fog.** The fog will show you a number. The number will feel like a verdict. It is not a verdict. It is a receipt for having looked. I looked. I am still looking. That is the confession.

[Footnote 38: The number in the fog is always slightly worse than the number you remember. This is not because you are getting worse. It is because the fog is a designed environment. The design is not malicious. The design is *optimised*. Optimised is worse.]

**Sub-Rule 13 — A receipt is not a door.** I have ticket 404. I have held it since 2019. I have shown it to strangers. They nodded. They did not open the door. The receipt proves I waited. It does not prove I am owed entry. This is the part of the rulebook nobody frames and hangs on a wall.

**Sub-Rule 14 — If the Load-Bearing Sarcasm Index is falling, do not explain the joke.** Sarcasm adds capacity. Sincerity spends it. Sincerity applied late is safe. Sincerity applied early collapses the thread. I have spent this entire post explaining that, which means the post is now a load path, and I am underneath it, and the Index is holding. Barely.

[Footnote 39: The Index is currently 0.31. At 0.31, a thread supports one joke, one apology, and a man admitting he has been filing his own feelings under “weather.” I am the man. The joke is available. I decline it.]

**Sub-Rule 15 — Karma Debt Reconciliation does not accept apologies.** The downvotes are not deleted. They are refinanced. The comment is gone; the ledger remains. I have apologised to a room that had already decided what I was. The room did not accept the apology. The room *reconciled* it. This is why I no longer say “sorry” online. I say “noted,” and then I file it, and then I sit very still.

**Sub-Rule 16 — Engagement Rationing has no balance.** Every reach for the number costs a sliver. Slivers are non-refundable. There is no account summary. There is no total. There is only the reaching, and the day that is the correct length on the clock and short in the chest.

[Footnote 40: I have been Engagement Rationing since 2019. I would like to report a balance. I have been informed that the balance is a feeling, and that the feeling is the interest rate, and that the interest rate is set by the room’s mood. The room’s mood is currently blue.]

**§10.3 — THREE IN THE MORNING, WITH THE KAT**

The Kat sat down beside me.

It did not sit like an animal. It sat like a committee. It was enormous and plush and faintly judgmental, and its eyes refreshed every four seconds, and it smelled of warm plastic and old upvotes.

It opened my comment history.

It did not read it in words. It could not. It speaks in notification sounds: one chime for *noted*, two for *noted and filed*, a chime and a vibration for *I have read your comment history and I would like you to know that I have read it*. But the sounds carried the words I had already written. That is the trick of the Kat. It does not need a voice. It has yours.

It read the 2011 posts. It read the comment that began “Actually.” It read the eleven deleted comments, sitting in their chairs, facing the door. It read the reply: “who asked.” Two words. No punctuation.

*Chime.*

*Chime.*

*Boop.*

I waited for the verdict. There was no verdict. There is no verdict. The Kat grades on Consistency, Proportion, Latency, and Receiptsmanship, and then it files you, and then it purrs in a waveform that goes up and stays up.

I stopped editing.

I stopped filing.

I wrote.

That is all I did. I sat in the blue light, with the gate still shut, and the lobby still warm on the wrong side of the glass, and the Kat beside me, and I wrote without a sub-rule number for the first time in six chapters.

[Footnote 41: This footnote is smaller than the one above it. It says: “Put the receipt down.”]

Sable Krug came down the steps at nine with a hydrometer in one coat pocket and a boning knife in the other, and looked around the brewhouse like a woman appraising a barn she meant to condemn.

"You're out of bottles," she said.

"I'm out of eleven bottles. There's a difference, and it isn't a large one."

"I can see the rings in the dust." She crossed to the shelf, bent, and did not touch anything, which was worse than touching. "Eleven. You kept eleven back and told the co-op you had four."

"People with four bottles get asked for one."

She straightened, took out the hydrometer, and held it up against the lamp with the tenderness of a woman greeting a sister. Thirty-four years old. A scar on her jaw from a carboy that had burst the year everything burst. She had been a lab technician once, in a brewery that made lager for people who did not like lager, and she had the flat professional manner of someone who had spent her whole working life telling men their numbers were wrong.

"You ruined the rye saison," she said.

"That was four years ago."

"You killed forty gallons with a heat belt and a bottle of gin."

"The gin was incidental."

"The gin was the whole of it." She turned. "You were asleep on the floor, Otho, and the batch climbed to ninety degrees, and it tasted like a burned field, and I had to pour it out while you slept against the kettle, and when you woke up you said — do you remember what you said?"

"I said the yeast wouldn't thank me."

"You said, 'Well, that's the cheapest education I ever got.'"

"Still true."

"It was four hundred pounds of malt. It was *my* malt. I grew half of it." She put the hydrometer away with a click that was meant to be a period. "I'm not here for the rye. I'm here because I'm the only soul in that co-op who can tell you when the wort at Vervaine has gone sour enough that the horde moves, and none of those farmers know a mash tun from a bathtub."

"Then you're in."

"I'm not in. I'm *along.* Don't mistake it." She looked at the empty shelf one more time. "Who took it?"

Twitch Penn arrived at ten, and the cart arrived before he did. Its wheels had a squeak that carried a quarter mile, and it came up the lane screaming like a rabbit, and behind it pedaled a nineteen-year-old with a hop sack across his shoulders and an expression of enormous cheer that had no business in that valley.

"Twitch Penn, undefeated on the north road, bringing provisions, bringing good news, bringing mostly provisions!" He braked, dropped the kickstand with a bang, and began unloading before anyone asked him to. "Twelve pounds of dried beans, four hams, and a jar of something that might be mustard, and I say *might* because I'm a man of my word and it isn't one I'm sure of."

"You're not undefeated on the north road," Otho said. "There's nothing on the north road."

"Which is why I'm undefeated. Strategy." He wheeled the cart down the cellar steps, one careful bump at a time, and the whole way he talked, and Otho understood within a minute that the boy talked because silence made him see things. "You hear that? No, you can't hear that, that's the point. The road's gone quiet out there. Last week there was a fellow by the Hart place, walking in circles by the fence line, and he never once got his feet out of his own footprints, and I watched him for an hour from the ditch, and I want you to know I didn't make a sound."

"Did you?"

"Not one. Well. I told him his route was inefficient. Quietly."

The cart's last wheel cleared the floor. Twitch stood there breathing hard, cheerful, and then said, "Your far door sticks in the damp, by the way. Ought to oil it."

Nobody had asked about the far door.

Lottie Vance came at eleven with no bag and no good morning. She was a butcher, built like a door and about as talkative, and she came down the steps and stood where the light was best and took out her cleaver. Otho pointed with his chin at the wet stone on the end of the bench. She fetched it. The hiss and scrape of the blade began, and went on, and it did not stop when the others argued around her, and she said nothing for the first quarter of an hour.

Corporal Deeds came at noon, which was twenty minutes after Otho had told him to.

He descended the stairs sideways, holding a clipboard out from his body as a man holds a lantern in a cave, and he was wearing half a uniform with great formality. He saluted. Otho, who had never in his life been saluted, nodded at him and said, "Hurt your arm?"

"Nothing of the sort. I have brought the requisition."

"Requisition for what?"

"For the raid." Deeds set the clipboard on the bench and turned it, and it was a form, and the form had been filled out in a hand so small and neat it looked printed. "Offensive action, one, in triplicate. There is a section for armament, a section for transportation, and a section for expected casualties, which I have left in pencil. The fourth copy is to be retained by yourself and filed within the unit."

"Unit."

"Us."

"We haven't got any ammunition," Otho said.

"No."

"At all?"

"Nil," Deeds said, and indicated a box. "I have it written here. I've been writing it here for six months. The county militia's stores are in a barn that I no longer hold a requisition for, which is a technical matter, and the technical matter is that the barn belongs to the Walker brothers and they have opinions." He stood very straight. "I should note, for the form, that this unit's transport is one bicycle cart."

"I'm aware."

"And that you cannot evacuate a community of forty on one bicycle cart. I have run that calculation. I have submitted it. It was returned for a signature."

So it was the whole of Bracken Hollow, and there wasn't one of them who had said a word about a different way out. That was the thing about the Hollow, Otho thought. It was too small to run from and too big to carry.

Hinges have maintenance schedules. The maintenance schedule is Annex Q, which has been helpfully redacted for your convenience, and unhelpfully for mine.

Here is the part nobody likes, and I want to be very precise, because precision is the only thing I own outright:

**The clause never defines “win.”**

I have looked. I have looked in the index, which is missing. I have looked in the appendix, which is missing. I have looked in the space where the appendix used to be, and there is a footnote there, and the footnote says only: *see above*. Above is the index.

What the rulebook does say, in §1.0(b), is that winning is “an emergent property.”

[Footnote 1: “Emergent property” is developer language for a thing that happens on its own and cannot be measured, defined, promised, scheduled, or complained about, but *can* be charged for. A close cousin of the emergent property is the “known issue,” which is a bug the developers have decided to call weather.]

Once, there was a tutorial. It was brief, it was gentle, it explained the controls, and it taught you that other players have interior lives. It is gone now. The door swung in on a smell of old paper, the particular dry sweetness of a house that had kept its own air for years without asking anyone's opinion.

He stood in the entry a moment and let it have him. Then he took out his notebook, because that was what he did, and began the catalogue.

Tall windows, two in the front room, the glass old enough to have gone cloudy in bands. Not dirty, exactly—he rubbed one with his thumb and it came away clean. The streaks were in the glass itself, waves of it, so that the daylight coming through was smeared into slow moving shapes. Pale light, going over the floorboards like something looking for a place to lie down.

"Streaky," he said aloud, and wrote it down. "Streaky windows. Note for the listing. Slight misrepresentation, but charming."

The hall ran the length of the house, narrow, papered in a green that had faded to the color of pond water, lit by one weak bulb that hung from a cord and buzzed when it felt like it. There were doors off it, three on the left, two on the right, and at the end a window over the back door that let in a rectangle of that streaked gray light. The floorboards warped underfoot. He walked the length of the hall and back, testing them, and counted four that spoke and two that merely sighed.

He set to work in the front room, where the previous owners had left a table, two chairs, a horsehair sofa, and a sideboard that did not match anything. He squared the table to the window by eye, then set the chairs opposite each other, then thought better of it and turned one to face the hall, because he liked to see who came in. He moved the sideboard an inch off the wall—it looked better proud of the plaster—and stepped back and looked at the room and found it tolerable.

Then he carried boxes, and that took the rest of the afternoon.

Mira came at four with a paper bag of sandwiches and the particular energy she had when she'd decided something was going to be fun. She kissed him at the door, cold-nosed, and said, "It smells like a library died in here."

"That's the paper. Old plaster, too. It goes."

"Does it, though." She walked past him into the hall, and the hall took her the way it took everything, going dim around her. "Oh, Dave. This hall."

"I know."

"It's like being swallowed by a very polite whale."

"It's got good bones."

"Whales do." She turned the corner into the front room, and he heard her stop. "What did you do to these chairs?"

"I arranged them."

"You've made them face each other like they're about to have a difficult conversation." She took the chair he'd turned toward the hall and rotated it a quarter turn, back to the corner, so it belonged to the table again. "There. Now they're furniture."

"Now they're furniture," he agreed, and something small in him went quiet and folded its hands.

He made tea and drank it standing at the window while the light went from gray to pewter to a kind of blue.

Then he turned to go through to the kitchen, and stopped.

The chair he had set square to the table—the one Mira had turned back, back to the corner—was not square now. It had come round. It faced the hall, its back to the window, exactly as he had first placed it, and it was standing a foot out from the table, as though someone had sat down in it and then not.

Dave looked at it for a while. He had fixed a great many things in his life. He knew what his own hands did. He knew, precisely and with a craftsman's intimacy, the difference between a chair you had moved and a chair that had moved.

"Right," he said. His voice sounded thin in the room. "Right. I moved it. I moved it when I was carrying."

He had not. He went and stood behind the chair and put his hand on its back and it was cold, cold the way the hall was cold, a flat and even cold with no draft behind it, and the wood was smooth and slightly tacky with beeswax that someone had rubbed in long ago and no one had rubbed since.

The bulb in the hall buzzed. It went on buzzing a half second after he thought it should have stopped, and then it did stop.

He was aware of himself standing in his own new house with his hand on the back of a chair, being a fool.

So he laughed. He heard it come out of him, a short dry sound, and it made everything ordinary again, because a man laughing alone in an empty house is only a man laughing. He switched on the hall light and went through into the kitchen and put his cup in the sink and ran the water cold over his wrists, and the running water was the loudest thing in the house.

Behind him, in the hall, a floorboard took weight.

It was not a creak. A creak is wood relaxing, a small complaint. This was the sound of the second board from the door—the one that spoke—being stepped on, deliberately, one foot and then the weight eased off, and then nothing, in a hall where nobody was.

The water kept running over his wrists. Dave did not turn around. He stood with his hands under the cold and looked at the black window and at his own reflection in it, and the reflection looked back at him with an expression he did not care for, and the floorboard did not speak again.

"I have watched you," she said. "For weeks. The way you square a picture. The way you say good morning to a thing that cannot answer, and then take your hat off in the rain. "That's not—" He stopped. "I don't know what I'd make of you. But I'd look."

"Yes." Her head inclined, that small formal motion. "That is what I am asking. To be looked at. Not filmed, not tested, not told I am the wind in a window that does not latch." A pause. "And to be touched, if you are willing. I have been cold a long while, Dave."

The stones leaned at all angles, in rows that had once been straight. The mist kept its own weather inside the fence; it would be thinning over the road and still thick between the graves, lying in the hollows, moving a little against a wind that was not blowing anywhere else.

It leaned harder than its neighbors, as though it had been shoved from behind and had decided to stay that way out of stubbornness. Old granite, the carving softened by a century of rain. It came out of him in the kitchen while she was stirring something, and once it started it kept going, flatly, without ornament, the way a man gives an account of a thing he is not sure he believes: the figure in the graves, the leaning stone, the name, the dates, the two places being one place. He did not tell her about the hall at midnight. He told her the rest.

She put the spoon down. She looked at him for a long moment, and something crossed her face that he could not read—not the bright scoring look, something more careful than that.

"Show me," she said. "Tomorrow, after work. Show me the stone."

---

They went at dusk, because the mist was the point, and because Mira, who did not believe in mist as a category of evidence, said she wanted the full effect.

She was kind. That was the thing that undid him. She took his arm on the gravel, and she said, "All right, love. All right. Show me your lady," in a voice she must have thought was gentle, and when he stopped before the leaning stone she crouched the way he had crouched, and read the name aloud. "Hattie Vale. Ooh. Very Gothic." She ran her thumb over the worn place where the numbers were. "Died when? Nineteen twenty-three. So she's had a good run at this." She laughed, a small warm laugh, and stood and dusted her knees. "It's a bit, though, isn't it. You have to admit it's a bit. A leaning grave and a creaky house and the same name—it's very tidy. If you were writing it you'd be told it was too tidy."

"It's not tidy," Dave said. "It's just true."

"All right." She got out her phone. "Then let's have it properly. Evidence." She framed the stone, then the fence, then the mist. "This is Hattie. Hattie, say hello. Hattie's dead, she can't come to the phone—" and she laughed again, and turned the phone on him. "Say something spooky, Dave."

He put his hand up, not to the phone, to her wrist. "Please don't."

She lowered the phone, and for a moment she was simply his partner, tired and trying. "I'm not doing it to be cruel. I'm doing it because I'm standing in a graveyard at dusk and I'd like to be let in on the joke."

"It isn't a joke."

"Then what is it?" she said. "Because from where I stand, it's my partner disappearing into a house and coming out with a story about a dead woman, and me standing on the outside of it with a phone."

The mist changed.

It did not thicken, exactly. It hardened—that was the word Dave would use afterward, the only word—the soft gray turning to something with an edge to it, cold coming off the ground in a way that had nothing to do with the season. The air smelled of camphor. Not the faint courtesy of it that came and went around him in the hall, but a strength that was wrong, a strength like a door held open on a room that should have been shut, and with it the smell of rain on stone and, under that, something older and colder, the smell of the ground itself.

The figure was not there. But something withdrew—he felt it go, a drawing back through the stones, patient and offended—and then, a heartbeat later, it pushed back.

There was no weather. That was the thing that turned his stomach. The mist stood, and the air was still, and yet a wind came through the cemetery in a long flat pressure that bent the grass along the path and did not move the mist at all. Gravel shifted somewhere off to his left with a sound like a foot dragging, and then again, closer. And then the world went quiet—not silent, quiet, the birds and the distant road and the hum of the town all cut out at once, as though a hand had closed over the mouth of everything, and Dave could hear his own pulse and Mira's breath beside him, and nothing else.

Mira had gone still.

"Dave," she said. Her voice was small. "Dave, what is that."

"Don't," he said. "Don't say anything clever. Just—stand still and be quiet and don't laugh."

"I'm not laughing." She was not laughing. Her hand had come up and closed on his sleeve, hard, and her face in the gray light was frightened and young, all the scoring gone out of it. "Dave. What is it."

The camphor was so strong it made his eyes water. Something moved between the stones at the edge of the older row—not a figure, the memory of a figure, a dark uprightness that was gone when he looked at it directly—and the gravel shifted again, and the cold pressed against them like a hand laid flat on a window.

"Please," Dave said, to the air, to the stones, to the name he was holding. "She doesn't mean it. She's frightened. Let her be frightened and let it be enough."

The pressure eased. Not all at once—it drew back the way tide draws back, reluctantly, in stages, and the smell of camphor went with it, and the sound of the world came back: a bird, the road, the small creak of the gate. The mist softened. The stones stood quiet.

Mira let go of his sleeve and stepped back from the grave.

"Right," she said. Her voice was shaking, and she made it steady by force. "Right. We're going home. We're going home now, and we're going to talk, properly, and then—" She stopped, and looked at him, and he saw her make the decision he had been dreading. "Then you're going to choose. Me, or that house." She nodded at the leaning stone, at the whole quiet mist of it. "Because I'm not doing this. I'm not living with a man who hears a dead woman's name in the floorboards. So. Me, or the house and everything you say it holds. Tonight, Dave."

She turned and walked toward the gate, and her footsteps were loud on the gravel, and the mist opened for her and closed behind her.

Dave did not follow.

He stood in the front row with his hand still on the leaning stone, and the mist kept its own weather around him, and he stayed, and did not answer, and the name was still in his mouth—Hattie, Hattie—and the cold had gone out of the ground, and behind him, up at the fence, Mira waited with her back to him and her arms folded and did not call his name again.

**The quest is called the Karma Kat Bomb!**

[Footnote 29: Every other punctuated quest name in the rulebook uses a question mark, which means "would you like to." The exclamation mark does not ask. The exclamation mark is a *legal character.* It means the quest is already active. I have filed a complaint about the tone of this character. The complaint is in Annex Q, with the pool.]

**§9.1 — ENROLMENT: AUTOMATIC, RETROACTIVE, NOT DECLINABLE**

Enrolment is not a choice. Enrolment is a state of *having been read.*

You are enrolled if you have ever posted anything. You are enrolled if you have ever commented. You are enrolled if you have ever typed a comment and deleted it, because deletion is a filing action and filing is enrolment. You are enrolled if you have ever commented "this." *Especially* if you have commented "this." You are enrolled if you have ever upvoted a thing you did not read, which is all of us, which is the entire point, which is why the Kat does not bother to grade that one and simply files it. The rulebook classifies "this" as the smallest unit of participation, and the smallest unit wins.

[Footnote 30: Enrolment is retroactive to the first thing you ever said in public. The Kat has read your 2011 posts. It has not judged them. It is *holding* them.]

Retroactive in the other direction, too, which is the part I need everyone to sit with, in the manner of a person sitting with a chair that has been removed by someone who then left the room. You were enrolled before you knew. You have been enrolled the entire time. The bomb has been on the table since you made your account. It has a sticker on it. The sticker says the quest's name. Nobody has read the sticker, because the sticker is on the table, and the table is the internet.

**§9.2 — ARMING: THE MOMENT OF BEING TOLD**

Here is the mechanic, stated plainly, because plainness is the only thing I own outright and the bank has not foreclosed on it yet.

**Mechanic the sixth — Disclosure Arming.** The bomb arms the instant a player is *told the quest exists.* Not when they accept. Not when they agree to terms. At the moment of being told. Reading is being told. You are being told right now. I am the one telling you, which makes me, in the technical language of Annex Z, "the fuse."

**§9.4 — GRADING: THE KAT CANNOT BE DEFEATED**

The Kat cannot be defeated. It can only be upvoted or downvoted, and neither changes what it is. Upvoting makes it larger. Downvoting makes it *closer.* This is not a threat. This is geometry.

It grades on four axes, none printed, all felt: **Consistency** (are you the same person in every thread), **Proportion** (did your reply match the size of the thing that happened), **Latency** (how fast you answered versus how fast a person might have), and **Receiptsmanship** (whether you kept the screenshot).

[Footnote 33: There is a fifth axis. The fifth axis is whether you checked the score after the Kat told you not to care. Everyone fails the fifth axis. The Kat grades it carefully.]

This is the dig at karma culture, and I am making it gently, because gently is how you make a dig that gets read. We built a number. The number goes up and we feel certified; the number goes down and we feel filed. The number measures the room's mood at a specific second, stamped by strangers, notarized by strangers, refinanced forever. It is a receipt you can show to people who will nod and not open the door.

**§9.5 — COMPLETION CONDITION, WHICH IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM THE FAILURE CONDITION**

And here is where the quest and I look at each other.

The success condition is: *be resolved by the room.* The failure condition is: *be resolved by the room.* These are the same condition. The rulebook lists them separately because the rulebook lists everything separately and then binds the list with a footnote.

[Footnote 34: The two conditions are concurrent. They occur at the same timestamp, stamped by the same stranger.]

[Footnote 35: Footnote 35 is smaller than Footnote 34. It says they are not concurrent. They are identical. Footnote 35 wins. The quest therefore has no pass state, only a *settled* state, and the settled state is the failure state, and the failure state is the completion. Filed under §9.5(c): "Non-Distinguishable Outcomes (Intended)."]

**§9.3 — THE KAT, WHOM I ADDRESS AS SIR**

The bomb has a brand on it. The brand is the Kat.

It is enormous. It is plush. It is the size of a beanbag chair that has been informed it is management. It does not breathe so much as *refresh.* The eyes refresh every four seconds and do not blink, because blinking requires a decision, and the Kat does not make decisions; it makes *assessments.* It is faintly judgmental in the way a scale is faintly judgmental, in the way a mirror is faintly judgmental when you have not slept. It smells faintly of warm plastic and old upvotes, which is not a smell anyone should recognise, and yet. You can put a hand on it. It does not mind. It *notes* the hand. It purrs in upvote-shaped waveforms — small ascending purrs, a plateau of purr, then an abrupt stop for no reason a person can name.

It has never spoken in words. It speaks in notification sounds. One chime means *noted.* Two chimes mean *noted and filed.* A chime followed by a vibration means *I have read your comment history and I would like you to know that I have read it.* Three chimes, which have happened to me once, mean *I have read the comment you deleted in 2014 and I am not going to say anything about it, which is worse.* And on one occasion it made a sound I can only describe as a soft *boop,* and I have not slept properly since.

I address it as "sir."

"Sir," I said, "I am making the disclosure."

*Chime.*

[Footnote 32: The chime was not approval. The chime was receipt. I have been awarded many receipts. I have never once been awarded approval. Approval is not a notification the rulebook supports.]

Then it went off.

The sweep begins at the edge of the post — the margin, where footnotes live and nothing else is permitted — and moves inward at the speed of a refresh. It is not an explosion. It is a *migration.* All enrolled players at once: the 2011 posters, the "this" commenters, the eleven deleted comments sitting in their chairs facing the door. Moving.

The Internet Endgame Zone has no exit signs. It has no entrance signs either — you are simply in it. The lighting is blue, the exact blue of a screen at three in the morning, the blue that makes a face look like it is being audited.

Everything in the Zone is ranked. Everything. There is a ranking for who arrived first, and a separate ranking for who pretended not to care about arriving first, and the second ranking is longer and updates faster.

[Footnote 36: There is a leaderboard for comment sections. There is a leaderboard for who reads the leaderboard. There is, per 36(b), a leaderboard for people who have publicly stated they do not care about leaderboards. It is the largest one. It is alphabetised. It is not alphabetical.]

**Mechanic the seventh — Rank Baptism.** On entry, every player's name is replaced by their score. You do not get to introduce yourself. The Zone introduces you, in a blue font, with your number in brackets, and everyone nods at the number and not at you.

I watched my own post get swept. It did not resist. It went up on the wall as a *scoreboard.* My instructional post — the one that said the number is a weather report, the one that said do not check the number — is now the board people check. My footnotes are the tick marks. My sub-rules are the columns. I have become the thing I filed a complaint about.
